1 Executive Summary In order to strengthen the Union’s framework for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT), Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) aims to harmonise the preventative measures to be put in place at Union level.

Articles 16 and 17 AMLR cover the regulatory obligations regarding the design and implementation of group-wide AML/CFT frameworks, including their application across cross-border group structures and in situations where branches or subsidiaries operate in third countries. The purpose of the mandates under Articles 16(4) and 17(3) AMLR is to clarify further these obligations in draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS).

The draft RTS contain requirements that specify further the framework and content of group-wide requirements. In addition to minimum general requirement, the draft RTS define provisions related to information sharing among entities of a group. Furthermore, they provide criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in cases of two or more obliged entities in the Union belonging to a head office in a third country and they are not in a parent/subsidiary relationship. They also provide conditions to apply group-wide requirements to structures other than groups and criteria to identify the head of the structure in these cases. This extension represents a significant development, particularly for the nonfinancial sector where such arrangements are common. The draft RTS ensure a proportionate and riskbased approach, ensuring applicability across both financial and non-financial sector groups. The mandates under Articles 16(4) and 17(3) AMLR are inherently interlinked, reinforcing each other through cross-reference obligations and complementary requirements. AMLA therefore proposes to draft a single set of draft RTS to address both mandates in a cohesive and simplified manner. Such a single instrument ensures regulatory coherence, avoids duplication between related provisions and provides obliged entities with a clearer and more consistent framework for implementing group-wide AML/CFT requirements across the Union.

In preparing this final report, AMLA sought and considered input from national supervisors across both financial and non-financial sectors and engaged with private sector representatives. AMLA further enhanced the final report by considering the responses provided by respondents collected through the public consultation conducted between 16 April and 15 June 2026.

These draft RTS are part of a broader set of AMLA instruments that will be delivered and that will touch upon the AML/CFT requirements of obliged entities. AMLA will continue its endeavors to place proportionality and the risk-based approach at the heart of this work and ensure the effectiveness of the instruments to be delivered while simplifying AML/CFT compliance for obliged entities where possible.
1.1 Next steps The draft RTS will be submitted to the European Commission for adoption before being published in the Official Journal of the European Union.

2 Background and rationale

2.1 General provisions Article 16 AMLR establishes the core obligations for group-wide AML/CFT frameworks, requiring parent undertakings to implement uniform policies, controls and procedures across all entities under their responsibility. It also mandates the establishment of a group compliance function and the adoption of an annual report on the implementation of these group-wide policies. Finally, it requires effective sharing of information within entities of a group. Article 16(4) AMLR requires AMLA to develop draft RTS specifying:
▪ the minimum requirements of group-wide policies, procedures and controls, including minimum standards for information sharing within the group;
▪ the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the cases covered by Article 2(1), point (42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

▪ the conditions under which the provisions of Article 16 AMLR apply to entities that are part of structures which share common ownership, management or compliance control, including networks or partnerships, as well as the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in those cases.

Article 17 AMLR complements the group-wide framework established under Article 16 AMLR by addressing situations where branches or subsidiaries located in third countries cannot fully implement group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls due to restrictions in local laws applicable in a third country. Article 17 AMLR requires parent undertakings or obliged entities to implement additional measures where legal or regulatory restrictions in a third country prevent compliance with the AMLR and to inform the supervisor of the home Member State of such impediments. Where those measures are insufficient to effectively manage the risk of ML/TF, supervisors of the home Member State may require the implementation of further supervisory actions, including restrictions on business relationships, the termination of transactions, or the closure of operations in the relevant third country. Article 17(3) AMLR therefore mandates AMLA to develop RTS specifying:
▪ the type of additional measures to be taken by obliged entities where the law of a third country prevents compliance with the AMLR,
▪ the minimum actions that must be implemented in such circumstances, and
▪ the additional supervisory actions that may be applied by supervisors where the measures taken are insufficient.

The provisions in the draft RTS fulfil the mandates in Articles 16 and 17 AMLR and establish high-level balanced group-wide requirements, which are compatible with existing (financial sector) requirements and guidelines.
2.2 AMLA’s approach - focus on simplification

In developing these RTS and taking into account the feedback received during the public consultation, AMLA sought to establish a simplified, proportionate and risk-based framework under the AMLR whenever possible. In particular, AMLA aimed to reduce unnecessary complexity, regulatory burden and compliance costs by establishing a single horizontal framework applicable across obliged entities in both the financial and non-financial sectors.
To achieve this objective, AMLA:
▪ refrains from sector-specifying requirements where the AMLR already provides sufficient detail;
▪ maintains flexibility by setting out measures and options that obliged entities may consider when determining the most effective and proportionate approach to compliance;
▪ streamlines closely related requirements falling within AMLA's regulatory mandate;
▪ seeks to ensure consistency with existing supervisory expectations and established standards while reflecting AMLA's mandate under the AMLR and the feedback received from stakeholders
▪ establishes a transitory regime for the first application of notifications set in Sections 5 and 6 to supervisors.

In preparing these draft RTS, AMLA assessed the relevant provisions of the AMLR, the EBA's advice to the European Commission, as well as inputs received from public and private sector stakeholders. This assessment was undertaken to identify areas where further clarification, simplification or refinement was necessary to support the effective and consistent application of the AMLR. AMLA also engaged with national competent authorities from the financial and non-financial sectors, the European Commission, EBA and representatives of obliged entities. AMLA furthermore considered the feedback received through the public consultation conducted between 16 April and 15 June 2026 and refined the draft RTS where appropriate in light of the responses received. Definitions (Section 1) The draft RTS introduce a definition of the term ‘structure’ for the purposes of ensuring a consistent interpretation and application of the requirements set out in the draft RTS. Following the public consultation and AMLA’s further assessment of the draft RTS, several definitions included in the Consultation Paper have been removed. AMLA considered that these definitions were not necessary to achieve the objectives of the draft RTS, taking into account stakeholders’ feedback and the need to avoid unnecessary regulatory complexity.

Minimum requirements regarding group-wide policies, procedures and controls (Section 2) The draft RTS further specify the group-wide requirements referred to in Article 16 AMLR. Article 16 AMLR requires parent undertakings in the Union to ensure that policies, procedures and controls are implemented consistently across all branches and subsidiaries within the group. The draft RTS provide rules setting out a clear governance framework, including the allocation of responsibilities, reporting lines and arrangements between relevant functions to ensure that relevant information is shared effectively across the group. To support the effective implementation of these obligations, the draft RTS also clarify that group-wide policies and procedures should be appropriately documented, kept up to date and made available to supervisors upon request.

In light of the feedback received during the public consultation, AMLA streamlined and simplified this section of the draft RTS, while retaining the elements necessary to ensure the consistent and effective application of group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls.

Information sharing within a group (Section 3) Effective information sharing is a cornerstone of the draft RTS, reflecting the principles outlined by the EBA as part of its response to the Commission’s call for advice issued in October 2025. The draft RTS set a broad list of information that when relevant under the AML/CFT framework may be shared within groups, enabling obliged entities to detect and mitigate cross-border ML/TF risks more effectively. The draft RTS nonetheless make clear that such sharing must be conducted in line with certain standards such as on a “need to know” basis, with appropriate safeguards to ensure compliance with data protection regulation and ensuring confidentiality and security.

Additional provisions clarify the approach to the sharing of information to and from third countries when information sharing takes place from the perspective of obliged entities of the group in the Union. Following the public consultation, AMLA revised this section and moved the specific pieces of information to Annex I setting out the categories and types of information to be shared within a group. AMLA also amended the drafting of Section 3 to improve clarity and further reflect the principles of simplification and proportionality in the text, also in view of stakeholders’ comments. Legal impediments affecting branches and subsidiaries in third countries (Section 4) Groups subject to the AMLR frequently operate through branches or subsidiaries established in third countries. In some jurisdictions, local legal or regulatory frameworks may restrict the ability of OEs to implement group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls. Such impediments may arise, for example, from national data protection rules, banking secrecy provisions, restrictions on the sharing of suspicious transaction information, or limitations on access to customer or beneficial ownership information.

Article 17 AMLR establishes a harmonised Union-level framework for managing such situations. Where the law of a third country does not permit compliance with the AMLR, parent undertakings or obliged entities are required to implement minimum actions, including additional measures, to ensure that branches and subsidiaries effectively manage ML/TF risks.

The draft RTS build on the framework established by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758, while extending its scope to all obliged entities under the AMLR, including the non-financial sectors. This approach ensures continuity with the existing regulatory framework while updating it to reflect the broader scope and supervisory architecture introduced by the AMLR. However, the previous structure has been simplified and the mention to specific legal impediments has been removed along with the prescriptive additional measures for each one of those scenarios.

The draft RTS introduce provisions on additional supervisory actions and establish a structured escalation framework to be applied where supervisors determine, following a supervisory assessment, that the measures taken are insufficient to effectively manage the risk. Where risks arising from thirdcountry impediments are considered remediable, supervisors may require corrective measures, including the submission and implementation of risk-mitigation plans, and monitor their

implementation. Where risks are deemed unmanageable, the framework provides for stronger supervisory interventions, including restrictions on business relationships or occasional transactions, and ultimately the closure of some or all operations in the affected jurisdiction. Following the public consultation, AMLA simplified and streamlined Section 4 by reducing the number of articles from seven to three and removing the mention to specific legal impediments with rigid requirements. The revised structure aligns the provisions more closely with the AMLR mandate, with separate articles addressing minimum actions, additional measures and supervisory actions. This approach improves clarity, reduces complexity and further reflects the principles of simplification and proportionality underpinning the draft RTS.

Criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in cases of two or more obliged entities whose head office is located outside of the Union (Section 5) The draft RTS introduce criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in cases where two or more obliged entities established in the Union have a common head office located outside of the Union and where there is no parent-subsidiary relationship among the obliged entities (sister or affiliate entities).

The draft RTS provide a clear methodology for determining which obliged entity should be identified as parent undertaking and assume responsibility for group-wide requirements. The quantitative and qualitative criteria set in the draft RTS focus on decision-making powers, controls and risk management capacity, ensuring that the identified obliged entity is the best positioned obliged entity to enforce AML/CFT measures across the group as a parent undertaking. This also ensures that the identified obliged entity has the necessary resources and influence to implement and monitor compliance effectively.

To prevent regulatory uncertainty, the draft RTS introduce a notification obligation and supervisory assessment, requiring the obliged entity identified as the parent undertaking to notify its role to the relevant supervisor. This mechanism ensures transparency and allows supervisors to identify and address potential gaps in compliance oversight.

In light of the feedback received during the public consultation, AMLA streamlined and simplified this section of the draft RTS, while retaining the elements necessary to ensure the consistent and effective identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in the cases where there is no parent-subsidiary relationship among the obliged entities in the Union belonging to the same head office in a third country. Conditions for the application of group-wide requirements to structure sharing common ownership, management or compliance controls (Section 6) The draft RTS clarify the extension of the scope of group-wide requirements from traditionally defined groups under accounting or prudential regimes to structures that, while not formally organised as groups, exhibit characteristics that warrant similar AML/CFT requirements. This includes networks, partnerships, or franchises where the structure has two or more obliged entities that operate under common ownership, management, or compliance controls or a combination of them. The recitals, definitions, and criteria set out in the draft RTS are specifically designed to provide obliged entities, particularly those in the non-financial sector, with clear, actionable guidance to determine

whether they fall within the scope of these provisions. The objective is to effectively target structures where the application of group-wide AML/CFT measures is both necessary and proportionate. In addition to defining the scope of application, the draft RTS also provide criteria for identifying the head of the structure for these structures. The criteria are built mainly to recognise the powers and controls of one entity in the structure.

To maintain regulatory clarity, the draft RTS introduce a notification requirement to the supervisors and supervisory assessment. This mechanism ensures that supervisors are aware of the identified entity acting as head of the structure and can monitor compliance of group-wide requirements effectively in such structures. First notification to supervisors shall take place no later than six months after the application of the RTS.

Under justified circumstances and to recognise proportionality, the draft RTS address situations in structures where obliged entities identify a non-obliged entity as the head or where there are legal impediments for the identification of the head. The draft RTS introduce a supervisory mechanism that allows obliged entities not to identify the head of the structure under certain conditions to ensure that certain minimum group-wide requirements still apply to them. In case the permission is granted, the application of group-wide requirements would be limited to certain minimum group-wide requirements that obliged entities would mutually comply with without requiring group-wide steering of one designated obliged entity acting as head of the structure. First notification to supervisors shall take place no later than six months after the application of the RTS.

In light of the feedback received during the public consultation, AMLA clarified the provisions in this section of the draft RTS, while retaining the elements necessary to ensure the consistent and effective application of group-wide requirements to structures other than groups having common ownership, management, compliance control or a combination of them. In addition, AMLA recognized proportionality in the application of group-wide requirements to structure other than groups in the absence of a head of the structure being an obliged entity, while still ensuring minimum application of certain group-wide requirements in this situation.

of XXX supplementing Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 of the European Parliament and of the Council with regard to regulatory technical standards on group-wide requirements, on additional measures and additional supervisory actions related to obliged entities’ branches or subsidiaries in third countries (Text with EEA relevance) THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION, Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Having regard to Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2024 on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purposes of money laundering or terrorist financing1, and in particular Articles 16(4) and 17(3) thereof, Whereas:

(1) Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 aims for the harmonisation of the measures to be put in place to prevent money laundering, its predicate offences, terrorist financing and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions at the Union level, including when such measures are designed and implemented in groups or in structures other than groups when such structures fulfil the conditions set out in this Regulation. Minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls should be developed, implemented and applied at the group level in an adequate and consistent manner, while avoiding any risks of compromising anti-money laundering, counterterrorism financing as well as preventing the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions.

(2) Group-wide policies, procedures and controls should be designed to ensure consistency in the implementation of the group-wide requirements mentioned in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, for example by enhancing governance arrangements; the standing and role of the compliance manager and, where applicable, those of the compliance officer at the level of the group; the relations between the parent undertaking and the subsidiaries and branches in the Union and in third countries; and the development and implementation of group-wide risk assessments. In this context, internal controls should be understood in line with the terms used in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and other applicable sectoral Union rules.

(3) At the same time, group-wide policies, procedures and controls should not result in a derogation for the parent undertaking in the Union from implementing the entity-level policies, procedures and controls, including its entity-level risk assessment.
(4) Information sharing within groups is a key element of ensuring an appropriate understanding of money laundering risks, terrorist financing risks and risks of the non-

implementation and evasion of targeted financial sanctions. Information sharing should mitigate these risks, especially when they are associated with customers and transactions.

(5) A list of information that, when considered relevant for the purposes of the prevention of money laundering, terrorist financing and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions, can be shared is provided in Annex I to this Regulation. The type of information to be shared within the group should include, among other types, information on customers, transactions, services and activities, risk assessments, internal controls, independent audit functions, external audits, suspicious transactions or activity reporting, group-wide policies, procedures and controls, and interactions with supervisors and competent authorities. In any case, information sharing should take into account the requirements set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on information accompanying transfers of funds and certain crypto-assets and amending Directive (EU) 2015/8492 and any administrative act of the supervisors.

(6) Obliged entities should use the information shared by other entities in the group to make, among other things, informed decisions on customers, transactions and risk assessments, and to potentially restrict or refuse to enter into a new relationship, terminate existing business relationships or restrict or refuse to carry out the execution of occasional transactions in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. Furthermore, the information shared within the group should be used to prevent and mitigate money laundering, terrorist financing and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions and to inform the parent undertaking in the Union of the group-wide-level risk assessment.
(7) Information sharing should also include ad hoc sharing of newly identified relevant information related to the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions.

(8) The Union anti-money-laundering / countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) framework applies to a wide variety of obliged entities. Some obliged entities perform transactions; other obliged entities, such as real estate agents, lawyers and notaries, provide services or activities connected to transactions. For these obliged entities, informationsharing requirements should include sharing of information related to the provision of services or activities under the AML/CFT framework.

(9) Certain aspects of the implementation of the AML/CFT framework involve the collection, analysis, storage and sharing of data, including personal data. The processing of personal data should be permitted only for the purposes of the prevention and management of money laundering, terrorist financing and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions. In addition, information sharing should be subject to sufficient guarantees in terms of confidentiality, secure channels and data protection in line with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation)3 regarding the use of information and should fully respect fundamental rights.

(10) Sharing of information should be implemented in a manner proportionate to the relevancy of the request and be based on a need-to-know assessment. In any case, obliged entities should not be prevented from sharing any relevant information related to risks of money

laundering, terrorist financing or the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions as deemed appropriate.

(11) Obliged entities in the Union may share information with other entities of the group outside the Union. In such cases, the Regulation clarifies that in cases where there are restrictions or prohibitions on the sharing of information to third countries, the parent undertaking in the Union and the other obliged entities of the group in the Union need to assess the restrictions and prohibitions and communicate them to the supervisors in the Union. Similarly, in cases where restrictions or prohibitions on the sharing of information exist from third countries to the Union, including to supervisors in the Union, obliged entities in the Union need to assess restrictions or prohibitions and communicate them to the supervisors in the Union. In any case, obliged entities should take appropriate measures to address such restrictions or prohibitions on sharing information.

(12) There are circumstances where a group or an obliged entity operates branches or subsidiaries in a third country whose law does not permit the implementation of groupwide policies, procedures and controls on AML/CFT. This can be the case, for example, where the third country's data protection, banking secrecy or professional secrecy law limits the group's ability to access, process or exchange information related to customers of branches or subsidiaries in the third country. In such cases, the parent undertaking in the Union or the obliged entity should communicate these legal impediments to its supervisor and may notify the supervisor of multiple impediments within a single notification.

(13) In those circumstances, and in situations where the ability of supervisors to effectively supervise the group's compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 is impeded because supervisors do not have access to relevant information held at branches or subsidiaries in third countries, additional policies, procedures and controls are required to manage money laundering and terrorist financing risks effectively. These additional policies, procedures and controls may include obtaining consent from customers, which can serve to overcome certain legal obstacles to the implementation of group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls in third countries where other options are limited.

(14) The need to ensure a consistent Union level response to legal obstacles to the implementation of group-wide policies, procedures and controls justifies the imposition of specific minimum actions that obliged entities are required to take in those situations. However, the extent of such additional policies, procedures and controls should be proportionate and risk based.

(15) Parent undertakings and obliged entities should inform their supervisors that the extent of the additional measures they have taken is appropriate in view of the money laundering and terrorist financing risk. However, should the supervisor consider that the additional measures an obliged entity has taken are insufficient to manage that risk, the supervisor should be able to direct the obliged entity to take specific additional measures to ensure the obliged entity's compliance with its obligations regarding AML/CFT requirements. In order to ensure effective oversight and coordination, where a supervisor is a self-regulatory body, the public authority overseeing that body should be informed of legal impediments reported by obliged entities, the steps taken to address those impediments, any supervisory actions requested and any relevant developments arising thereafter.

(16) The additional supervisory actions described in this Regulation are specific to situations where, in the context of operations or activities carried out in a third country, including through branches or subsidiaries forming part of the group, the parent undertaking in the Union or the obliged entity do not put in place adequate systems and controls to manage the money laundering and terrorist financing risks where the law of that third country does

not permit the application of group-wide AML/CFT systems and controls that comply with Union law. The assessment of whether such third-country legal or regulatory impediments prevent effective compliance should not depend on the internal allocation of functions within the group. Where operations or activities are carried out in a third country through a branch or subsidiary, such assessment should be made irrespective of whether specific AML/CFT functions are performed locally or at the group level.

(17) Following a supervisory assessment, where the policies, procedures, systems and controls put in place do not ensure that the associated money laundering and terrorist financing risks are effectively managed, supervisors should apply the additional supervisory actions provided for in this Regulation. Those additional supervisory actions complement other supervisory actions and measures that supervisors may apply under Union or national law, including enforcement measures available under those legal frameworks. The actions supervisors take should be proportionate and risk based, taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

(18) The provisions of this Regulation should also be without prejudice to the enhanced due diligence measures obliged entities are required to take when dealing with natural persons or legal entities established in countries identified by the Commission as having significant strategic deficiencies in their national AML/CFT regimes, weaknesses in their national AML/CFT regimes or posing a specific and serious threat to the Union’s financial system pursuant to Articles 29, 30 and 31 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

(19) For groups whose head office is located outside of the Union, where at least two subsidiaries are obliged entities established in the Union and they are not in a relationship of control with each other pursuant to Article 2(1), point (42)(b), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, one parent undertaking in the Union, responsible for the implementation of the AML/CFT framework and the prevention to the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions, should be identified.

(20) In the situation covered by Article 2(1), point (42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, before notifying the supervisor, obliged entities in the Union should assess their role, taking into account certain criteria such as the prominence of activities, the understanding of operations and the responsibility of implementing group-wide requirements. Sufficient prominence of the obliged entities should be based on elements such as the type of obliged entity, cross-border establishments of any kind, the customer base, the amount of transactions when these are performed. In case such criteria are not enough to determine sufficient prominence of the obliged entities, other criteria should be the total annual turnover or the balance sheet or the average number of staff of the identified obliged entity in the group. Sufficient understanding of operations of the obliged entities should be based on qualitative criteria showing the types of powers and influence of the identified obliged entities in the group in the Union. In case such criteria are not enough to determine sufficient understanding of operations, an additional criterion should be the number of staff in the compliance functions referred to in Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

(21) To ensure that supervisors are aware of the identified obliged entity as parent undertaking in the Union for groups whose head office is located outside of the Union and that have two or more obliged entities in the Union which are not a subsidiary of another undertaking that is an obliged entity established in the Union, a notification and approval mechanism to supervisors should be established.

(22) The identified obliged entity in the Union pursuant to Article 2(1), point (42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 should submit a notification to the supervisor. The supervisor should be able to request, where necessary, specific clarifications or additional information regarding the parent undertaking assessment performed by the identified obliged entity.

The assessment should be based on whether the identified obliged entity fulfils the criteria set out in Article 2(1), point (42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

(23) All the supervisors and the Authority for Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (´the Authority´) should be fully informed in any case on the notification procedure to identify the parent undertaking in the Union pursuant to Article 2(1), point (42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. This is to ensure that appropriate information sharing and good cooperation between supervisors take place and that the supervisor adopts effectively and timely the decision on the identification of the parent undertaking in the Union. In cases of disagreement between supervisors on the assessment of the parent undertaking performed by the supervisor, one or more supervisors may ask the Authority to settle the disagreement between supervisors in cross-border situations.

(24) In addition to groups, structures exist, such as networks or partnerships or franchises, in which obliged entities might share common ownership, management, compliance control or a combination of them, which should be subject to group-wide requirements. To ensure a level playing field across the sectors whilst avoiding overburdening the affected sectors, this Regulation identifies situations where group-wide policies, procedures and controls, including information sharing requirements, should apply to those structures, taking into account the principle of proportionality.

(25) Given the different types of structures that could exist in different sectors and jurisdictions, especially in the non-financial sector, the conditions for the qualification of structures that share common ownership, management, compliance control or a combination of them should be designed in a general and comprehensible manner to ensure harmonisation at Union level. Furthermore, such conditions should be designed broadly to allow a wide application of the group-wide requirements. For instance, common compliance control should not be limited to compliance under the AML/CFT framework, but include other types of compliance such as any prudential, product and service compliance in place.

(26) Structures other than groups under the scope of this Regulation could be identified in specific forms such as networks, partnerships or franchises comprising two or more obliged entities. Networks are common arrangements for auditors, external accountants, lawyers and other professionals. These arrangements are established for specific purposes and can have common ownership, common management, common compliance control or a combination of them. Partnerships are also common arrangements for auditors, external accountants, lawyers and notaries. They can include obliged entities belonging to different categories and share common ownership, common management, common compliance control or a combination of them. Further, franchises are common arrangements for instance for professionals in sectors such as real estate (e.g. real estate agents) and gambling. Arrangements put in place under a common franchise may share certain elements of common management, common compliance control or a combination of them for the purposes of marketing specific types of goods and/or services. Under the conditions set out in this Regulation these structures should be subject to group-wide requirements.

(27) In addition, given the close operational and organisational links between legal entities and their branches, the application of group-wide requirements to such forms of structures is necessary to ensure a consistent and comprehensive approach to AML/CFT risk management throughout the Union. For instance, an obliged entity authorised in one Member State that operates in other Member States through one or more branches, even when it has no subsidiaries, should be subject to this Regulation. SECTION 1 GENERAL PROVISIONS Article 1 Subject and scope This Regulation lays down rules concerning:
(a) group-wide requirements in accordance with Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624;

(b) additional measures and supervisory actions to effectively handle the risk of money laundering and terrorist financing to which branches or subsidiaries of obliged entities in third countries may be exposed in accordance with Article 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

Article 2 Definitions For the purpose of this Regulation, in addition to the definitions set out in Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1620 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Article 2 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 of the European Parliament and of the Council, the following definition shall apply:
(1) ‘structure’ means any form of organisation, agreement or similar that:
(a) includes at least two obliged entities;
(b) is not a group within the meaning of Article 2(1), point (41) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624;

(c) has the objective of establishing a common framework of business, professional or commercial relationships having an element of duration connecting two or more obliged entities regardless of the legal form used;
(d) has common ownership, management, compliance controls or a combination of these elements.

SECTION 2 MINIMUM GROUP-WIDE REQUIREMENTS Article 3 Minimum requirements regarding group-wide policies, procedures and controls
1. The parent undertaking in the Union shall ensure that it complies with:
(a) the organisational requirements for the application of Section 1 of Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 by:

(i) setting up, implementing and maintaining an organisation and coordination framework at the group level with sufficient decision-making powers for the compliance manager at the level of the group and compliance officer appointed where justified by the activities carried out at the group level pursuant to Article 16(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. (ii) ensuring that the management body, internal controls and independent audit function have the necessary information at the group level to be able to carry out their functions under the applicable AML/CFT framework and to address and implement any administrative act issued by any supervisor for the oversight and management of entities and branches of the group in Member States and in third countries as applicable;

(iii) identifying and mitigating conflicts of interests between the prevention and management of risks related to money laundering, terrorist financing and the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions and the tasks of the commercial functions of groups, including at the entity and branch level as applicable as part of the risk management framework;
(b) the requirement to perform group-wide risk assessment by:
(i) ensuring that the group-wide risk assessment pursuant to Article 16(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 is commensurate to the complexity and the risk profile of the group;

(i) ensuring that the group compliance functions referred to in Article 16(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 have regular and documented information exchanges with the management body of the parent undertaking, commercial functions, other compliance functions established at entities and branches of the group as applicable, other internal controls and independent audit functions, and external auditors;

SECTION 3 INFORMATION SHARING Article 4 Information sharing within a group

1. For the purposes of the prevention of money laundering, terrorist financing and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions, the parent undertaking and the obliged entities within a group shall enable the sharing of the information listed in Annex I when relevant as referred to in Article 16(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

2. The sharing of information listed in Annex I within the group shall be provided to any obliged entity that is part of the group, taking into account the availability and quality of the information.

3. The parent undertaking shall define and maintain policies and procedures for information sharing within the group. Group-wide requirements shall not impose a requirement of the approval of the parent undertaking or any other obliged entity to share the information listed in Annex I to any obliged entity within the group.
Obliged entities within the group shall set up appropriate technical and organisational means through which such sharing can take place, taking into account size, complexity and risks.

4. Information shall be up to date, readily accessible, provided in an adequate and comprehensible form, provided on a need-to-know basis and be shared in line with the requirements stipulated by the applicable data protection legislation and in line with fundamental rights, through secure channels and respecting the requirements of security, integrity and confidentiality.

Information-sharing policies, procedures and controls shall include appropriate records of information exchanges to ensure the traceability and accountability of such information and to ensure effective supervision.

5. Information sharing within the group shall not affect the individual responsibility of each obliged entity to comply with AML/CFT requirements and to prevent the risk of the nonimplementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions. Each obliged entity of the group shall remain fully responsible for complying with due diligence requirements and performing its own risk assessments and making its own risk-related decisions, even when such decisions are based on information shared at the group level and taking into account any outsourcing, reliance on other obliged entities or other third-party arrangement in place.

SECTION 4 MINIMUM ACTIONS AND ADDITIONAL MEASURES FOR BRANCHES OR SUBSIDIARIES IN THIRD COUNTRIES OF OBLIGED ENTITIES AND PARENT UNDERTAKINGS IN THE UNION, AND SUPERVISORY ACTIONS Article 7 Minimum Actions

(a) inform the supervisor without undue delay, and, in any case no later than 28 calendar days from the identification of the legal impediment, of the following:

(ii) how the application of the law of the third country concerned does not permit or restricts the application of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624

3. Where the parent undertaking in the Union or an obliged entity cannot effectively manage the money laundering and terrorist financing risks by applying the measures referred to in paragraph 2, it shall ensure that the branch or subsidiary established in the third country implements such additional measures as necessary, appropriate and proportionate to effectively manage those legal impediments.

4. The parent undertaking in the Union or the obliged entity shall select and determine the extent of the additional measures referred to in paragraphs 2 and 3 using a risk-based approach, shall without undue delay inform the supervisor of the additional measures taken and shall provide an assessment of their appropriateness in view of the money laundering risks, terrorist financing risks and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions.

(c) carry out enhanced reviews, including, where this is commensurate with the money laundering and terrorist financing risks associated with the operation of the branch or subsidiary established in the third country, carry out on-site checks or order the performance of independent audits, to be satisfied that the branch or subsidiary effectively identifies, assesses and manages the money laundering and terrorist financing risks;

(d) ensure that their branches or subsidiaries established in the third country seek prior approval from the senior management of the parent undertaking or the obliged entity for the establishment and maintenance of higher-risk business relationships, or for carrying out of higher-risk occasional transactions;

4.1 Impact assessment with cost-benefit analysis Introduction As per Article 49(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1620, before submitting draft regulatory technical standards (RTS) to the European Commission, AMLA shall conduct open public consultations and analyse the potential related costs and benefits.

This analysis presents the Impact assessment with cost-benefit analysis (IA/CBA) of the main policy options included in the Consultation Paper (CP) on the draft RTS under Articles 16(4) and 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

This IA/CBA is qualitative in nature and the policy choices have been taken primarily in accordance with qualitative considerations, taking into account the experience and professional judgment of competent authorities from the financial and the non-financial sector, self-regulatory bodies (SRBs), and AMLA, as well as input provided by the European Banking Authority (EBA) in its response to the European Commission’s Call for Advice and feedback received during the public consultation. Moreover, quantitative figures in relation to these mandates are currently unavailable and performing a targeted collection would impose a disproportionate burden on obliged entities. Where quantitative evidence is lacking, the analysis is supported by structured qualitative reasoning and professional judgement informed by supervisory experience and wider stakeholders’ input.
Background Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) mandates AMLA to draft RTS specifying minimum standards for group-wide policies and procedures, including:
▪ minimum standards for information-sharing within the group;
▪ the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking for groups whose head office is located outside of the Union; and

▪ the conditions under which the provisions of Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 apply to entities that are part of structures which share common ownership, management or compliance control, including networks or partnerships, as well as the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in those cases.

On 12 March 2024, the European Commission issued a Call for Advice to the EBA on certain draft RTS under the new EU anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) framework, to inform AMLA’s work. As part of it, the EBA was requested to provide technical advice and set out options for AMLA to consider when developing the draft RTS on group-wide policies and procedures under Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

In preparing these options, EBA drew on information from its prudential work and AML/CFT guidelines or standards where applicable. Within the scope of the mandate under Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, EBA focused solely on minimum standards for information sharing within groups that are

A. Problem identification The previous EU AML/CFT framework relied largely on the national transposition by Member States of the requirements set out in Directive (EU) 2015/849 and its subsequent amendments. This approach proved to be insufficient to effectively tackle the cross-border nature of financial crime, which requires an integrated and harmonised framework at Union level.

To strengthen the effectiveness of the Union’s AML/CFT efforts, group-wide requirements for obliged entities are an essential part in ensuring adequate risk assessment, overview of activities, risks, and controls at group level. By applying such requirements, obliged entities formed in groups or structures other than groups, are required to implement a minimum level of group-wide or group-wide equivalent policies, procedures and controls to prevent and manage ML/TF risks and the risks of nonimplementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions.

To bring AML/CFT rules to an efficient and uniform level across the Union, Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 introduces harmonised rules on group-wide requirements. This provision also refers explicitly to Articles 9 and 10 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, which contain requirements on internal policies, procedures and controls, as well as on business-wide risk assessment. Supervisory experience, however, shows that obliged entities structured in groups often face challenges in designing, implementing and reviewing group-wide policies, procedures and controls. Additionally, a fragmented approach to the scope of minimum group-wide requirements has been identified in some cases, particularly in the non-financial sector. To ensure a more consistent and effective application of group-wide policies, procedures and controls, clearer rules at EU level are needed. Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 does not address critical parts of group-wide requirements, in particular:
▪ minimum requirements on the scope of group-wide policies, procedures and controls;
▪ the type of information that could be shared within a group;

To prevent the misuse of the Union’s financial system for the purposes of ML/TF and to ensure the highest standard of protection for personal data of Union citizens, Article 17(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires parent undertakings to ensure that their branches and subsidiaries located in third countries comply with requirements laid down in that Regulation.

However, there may be circumstances in which the law of a third country prevents compliance with those requirements, for example due to limitations on a group’s ability to access, process or exchange information, resulting from insufficient level of data protection or banking secrecy law in that third country. In such cases, the parent undertaking or obliged entity shall take additional measures to ensure that branches and subsidiaries located in the third country effectively manage the ML/TF risks, associated with the obliged entity’s operations in that country.

Where the implementation of such additional measures is insufficient to effectively manage those risks, supervisors shall, following a supervisory assessment, apply one or more additional supervisory actions to ensure adequate risk mitigation and safeguard the integrity of the Union’s financial system. While the Regulation does not specify those additional measures and supervisory actions, Article 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires AMLA to develop draft RTS specifying them.

B. Policy objectives The objective of the mandate under Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 is to contribute to the strengthening of the harmonised AML/CFT framework applicable to obliged entities formed in groups or structures other than groups as provided in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, while adhering to the risk-based approach and the principle of proportionality.

To achieve this objective, the draft RTS specify minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls and establish the conditions under which group-wide requirements apply to obliged entities forming part of structures other than groups that share common ownership, management or compliance controls. For such structures, the application of those requirements ensures a level-playing field, while taking into account the need for their proportionate application to the nature of the business, risks, complexity and size of the structure. By establishing such minimum requirements, the draft RTS aim to address deficiencies in the application of group-wide requirements that could lead to the inconsistent application, or non-application, of group-wide requirements across the Union as well as to clarify certain situations applicable structures other than groups. In addition, the draft RTS address the minimum level of information sharing within groups, to ensure compliance with the obligations to mitigate ML/TF risks and the risks of evasion or circumvention of targeted financial sanctions (TFS). Given the evolving nature of ML/TF risks and the risks of non-implementation and evasion of TFS, the information-sharing framework should also remain sufficiently adaptive to ensure that relevant and emerging risk-related information can be effectively exchanged within groups.

Closely related to the mandate under Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 is the mandate under Article 17(3) of that Regulation. In this context, the draft RTS aim to ensure that ML/TF risks arising from operations of obliged entities with subsidiaries and branches in third countries are effectively identified, assessed and managed at group level, even where the legal framework of the third country prevents the full application of group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls. The draft RTS seek to address potential regulatory and supervisory gaps that may otherwise be exploited when branches or subsidiaries operate in jurisdictions with legal impediments related to data protection, banking secrecy, or supervisory access, thereby safeguarding the integrity of the Union’s financial system. To support this objective, the draft RTS promote a consistent and convergent approach to be applied by obliged entities across the Union. By specifying the types of minimum actions and additional measures, and establishing a common framework for supervisory actions, it seeks to minimize divergent interpretations and uneven application of risk mitigation requirements by obliged entities, while preserving the risk-based nature of the AML/CFT framework and ensuring proportionate implementation.

Further, the draft RTS aim to enhance supervisory effectiveness. By defining a framework of supervisory actions that may be applied where additional measures prove insufficient, the draft RTS support supervisors in responding in a timely, proportionate and risk-based manner to situations where ML/TF risks are not effectively managed. This includes enabling supervisors to require submission and implementation of a risk mitigation plan, enhanced monitoring, or, where risks are no longer manageable, restrictive or exit-type measures, thereby ensuring that supervisory intervention is aligned with the severity of the risks identified.

The draft RTS also address the identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in situations where two or more obliged entities are not in a parent-subsidiary relationship and have their head office in a third country. For such cases, Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 introduces a definition of parent undertaking in the Union by reference to qualitative criteria, namely the determination of sufficient prominence of activities of one obliged entity over the other(s), the sufficient understanding of activities of one obliged entity over the other(s) and if the obliged entity is given the responsibility to implement the group-wide policies, procedures and controls. The draft RTS therefore seek to substantiate these qualitative criteria by specifying how they should be assessed and applied in practice. They also provide for a notification and supervisory assessment process to support the consistent identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in those cases.

Furthermore, the draft RTS establish the conditions under which certain obliged entities organised in structures other than groups, such as networks, partnerships or franchises, and having common ownership, management or compliance controls, shall adopt, implement and apply group-wide requirements, taking into account the principle of proportionality. The draft RTS specify alternative minimum conditions for determining whether such structures fall within scope of common ownership, management or compliance control and provide that the group-wide requirements are applied

The draft RTS establish also a framework for the identification of the obliged entity that shall act as the head of the structure to ensure compliance with group-wide requirements applicable to the structure. C. Baseline scenario Under the baseline scenario, obliged entities would apply group-wide requirements solely under Articles 9, 10 and 16 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, without any additional provisions specifying those group-wide requirements. In particular, no additional provisions would clarify the type of information to be shared within a group, the identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in the case of Article 2(1)(42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, or the conditions under which group-wide requirements apply to entities forming part of structures other than groups that share common ownership, management or compliance control.

The lack of regulatory provisions in this context might lead to divergent design and implementation of group-wide requirements across sectors and Member States. It may also create uncertainty regarding the type of information to be shared within a group, the identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in the situation covered by Article 2(1)(42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, and the determination of the structures other than groups to which group-wide requirements apply and the proportionate application of those requirements. All these aspects would ultimately undermine the consistent application of group-wide requirements and create a risk of for regulatory arbitrage, as criminals might exploit jurisdictions with more permissive interpretations.

In addition, obliged entities would be required to apply minimum actions and additional measures to ensure that their branches and subsidiaries located in third countries where local law does not permit compliance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 effectively manage ML/TF risks, solely on the basis of Article 17 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, without any further specification of the types of additional measures and minimum actions to be taken. This might lead parent undertakings or obliged entities to take divergent approaches across different sectors and jurisdictions, thereby undermining the harmonisation objective pursued by the Union’s AML/CFT framework.

Similarly, competent authorities would assess the adequacy of the measures implemented by obliged entities and decide on the application of additional supervisory actions exclusively on the basis of Article 17 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and the provisions of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 as transposed into national law. However, no further harmonised Union-level framework would exist to define common supervisory actions. This might undermine supervisory convergence and create potential supervisory gaps that might be exploited for ML/TF purposes.

D. Options considered, cost-benefit analysis, and preferred option This section describes the main policy options considered and the decisions taken as part of the development of the draft RTS under Articles 16(4) and 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

This section starts by outlining the overarching principles guiding the policy decisions. Then, it presents the main policy options considered for each policy issue addressed by the draft RTS, followed by a qualitative analysis of the potential costs and benefits of each option, and concludes by identifying the preferred option resulting from the analysis.

Policy issue 1: level of granularity of minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires AMLA to specify minimum requirements for groupwide policies, procedures and controls. In determining the appropriate level of granularity of those requirements, AMLA considered the following options.
A. Adopting detailed minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls.
B. Adopting principle-based minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls.

Option A Under Option A, the draft RTS would specify minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls at a highly detailed level. The draft RTS would prescribe in a granular manner the elements to be included in group-wide policies, procedures and controls, including detailed governance arrangements, internal roles and reporting requirements. Such approach would aim to minimise interpretative differences by setting out comprehensive and prescriptive expectations applicable across all groups.

This option would contribute to a high degree of harmonisation and supervisory clarity, as obliged entities and competent authorities would rely on a common and detailed set of requirements. It could strengthen consistency of group-wide frameworks, particularly in complex cross-border groups, and facilitate supervisory assessments by reducing discretion in implementation. However, this option would entail higher compliance and implementation costs, especially for smaller or less complex groups and for obliged entities operating across different sectors with diverse organisational structures and business models. Moreover, such approach could create unnecessary complexity, reduce the proportionate application of the draft RTS, limit obliged entities' ability to adapt group-wide arrangements to their organisational structures, business models and risk profiles, and increase the risk of regulating matters already addressed in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 or potentially extending beyond the scope of the mandate under Article 16(4) of that Regulation. Option B Under Option B, the draft RTS would specify minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls at a more principle-based level, focusing on essential elements necessary to ensure effective group-wide AML/CFT risk management. The draft RTS would set out the objectives and main components to be covered by group-wide frameworks, while leaving obliged entities sufficient flexibility to determine the level of detail and operational arrangements in light of their size, internal organisation, and risk exposure, subject to supervisory oversight.

By establishing minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls, rather than prescribing detailed operational rules, this option would ensure a consistent regulatory baseline across

different sectors while allowing obliged entities to implement those requirements in a manner proportionate to their size, organisational structure and ML/TF risk profile. This approach would define the regulatory outcome to be achieved without prescribing detailed implementation measures, thereby reducing unnecessary complexity and avoiding requirements that could potentially extend beyond the framework of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. It would also accommodate the diversity of groups and structures across sectors.

The public consultation, subsequent discussions with the European Commission and feedback from supervisors confirmed the appropriateness of this approach. In response, the draft RTS were further simplified, streamlined and reorganised into broader thematic areas by removing unnecessary definitions and provisions and improving the clarity and consistency of the drafting. These revisions strengthened alignment with Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, reinforced proportionality, and reduced implementation complexity, while preserving the effectiveness of the minimum group-wide requirements.

The main drawback associated with this option is that a lower level of granularity may result in some variation of implementation practices across obliged entities. Sectoral variations may also entail additional supervisory costs, as they would require increased reliance on supervisory judgment and coordination to ensure consistent outcomes. However, such sectoral variations are considered acceptable, given the need to provide a sufficient degree of flexibility to the wide range of obliged entities subject to Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

Preferred option Based on the considerations outlined above, Option B has been chosen as the preferred option, as it provides an appropriate balance between harmonisation, proportionality and flexibility in the specification of the minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls. By specifying those minimum requirements in a principle-based manner, rather than through detailed operational rules, Option B ensures the consistent application of the minimum requirements across all sectors, while allowing obliged entities to implement those requirements in a manner proportionate to their size, organisational structure and ML/TF risk profile. The revisions made following the public consultation further strengthened this approach by simplifying the framework, reorganising the minimum requirements into broader thematic areas to improve clarity and facilitate their application, and reinforcing its alignment with Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

Policy issue 2: the scope of information-sharing within a group Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires AMLA to specify minimum standards for information sharing within a group. The policy issue concerns how broadly the obligation to share information within groups and structures other than groups should apply and general standards on such sharing, in particular with regard to the type of information covered, the entities involved, and the legal and practical limits to information sharing, including data protection and confidentiality. For the specification of the scope of information that shall be shared, AMLA considered the following options:
A. A restrictive approach, defining a limited and exhaustive list of information that may be shared, accompanied by strict limitations on information sharing.

B. A broader approach, establishing a minimum non-exhaustive list of information that may be shared, complemented by specific safeguards for such sharing.

Option A Under Option A, the draft RTS would define the scope of information sharing within groups and structures other than groups through a closed and exhaustive list of information that obliged entities are permitted to share within a group or structures other than groups. It would also introduce limitations on the sharing of information, such as requiring information to be shared through the parent undertaking or restricting the circumstances in which information can be shared. The underlying logic of this approach would be to enhance legal certainty and uniformity by precisely delineating the information flows allowed for AML/CFT purposes, thereby limiting discretion at group level and reducing the risk of unlawful data processing.

The main benefit of this option is legal certainty. It would reduce instances of inconsistent interpretation and litigation, particularly in sensitive areas such as data protection and confidentiality. However, this option would introduce significant limitations to information sharing within groups. An exhaustive list would be inherently rigid and would not adequately reflect the evolving nature of ML/TF risks, limiting the ability of groups and structures to respond effectively to emerging threats, new typologies or specific group-level risk exposures. The draft RTS would need to be regularly amended to reflect emerging risks, resulting in additional implementation costs for obliged entities and reducing regulatory agility. Moreover, information that is materially relevant for AML/CFT purposes could fall outside the predefined scope, thereby weakening risk identification and mitigation. For instance, it could expose obliged entities within the groups or structures to the risk of reopening business relationships outside the group risk appetite or failing to identify suspicious activities due to lack of relevant information. Restrictions on the circumstances or channels through which information could be shared could also delay or prevent relevant information from reaching the obliged entity that needs it for AML/CFT purposes.

Option B Under Option B, the draft RTS would establish a minimum, non-exhaustive list of information that may be shared within groups, while allowing for additional information sharing where relevant for the prevention of ML/TF and the risk of non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions. This approach would be complemented by explicit safeguards, including compliance with data protection rules, confidentiality and the application of a need-to-know principle, as well as appropriate requirements concerning the security and integrity of information sharing. The overall objective of this approach would be to facilitate the timely and effective flow of relevant information within groups, with the aim of supporting the effective mitigation of ML/TF risk and the risk of non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions, while avoiding disproportionate information sharing. The benefits of Option B are threefold. First, it would support effective and timely group-wide risk identification and mitigation by ensuring that relevant information can be shared within the group if needed, without the constraints of an overly rigid framework. More specifically, obliged entities belonging to the group or structures other than groups would be allowed to share information among themselves, without limiting the sharing of information only through the parent undertaking or the head of the structure in the Union. Second, by linking the information-sharing framework directly to

Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and providing in Annex I a minimum list of information, this option would improve legal certainty while maintaining sufficient flexibility to address evolving ML/TF risks. Third, by embedding clear safeguards based, among others, on relevance, proportionality, the need-to-know principle, data protection and confidentiality, this approach would mitigate the risk of unlawful data sharing. In addition, by clarifying that each obliged entity remains individually responsible for complying with its obligations under Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, the draft RTS would ensure that information sharing supports, rather than replaces, entity-level AML/CFT compliance.

Compared with Option A, this approach would require obliged entities to exercise greater judgment in determining what information is relevant for AML/CFT purposes and in designing information-sharing arrangements appropriate to their organisational structure and risk profile. This may entail some initial implementation costs associated with reviewing or adapting internal policies, procedures, governance arrangements and information-sharing systems to ensure that the minimum requirements and safeguards are applied consistently across the group or structure. However, these implementation costs are expected to be offset by the legal certainty and adequacy in designing information-sharing arrangements appropriate to the organisational structure and ML/TF risk profile of groups and structures.

While this option may result in some variation in information sharing practices across groups or structures other than groups in different sectors and require greater supervisory judgment in assessing compliance with the minimum requirements, it would ensure that at least the essential scope of relevant information is shared within groups and structures across all sectors. Moreover, the draft RTS recognise a certain degree of flexibility in the way information sharing may take place to ensure that obliged entities can adapt the application of the draft RTS to their specific business models, as well as situational needs. This flexibility is reflected in the use of general standards rather than an exhaustive determination of the information that may be shared, or the circumstances and manners in which such sharing may take place.

At the same time, this flexibility would not affect the individual responsibility of each obliged entity for compliance with its AML/CFT obligations. Information received within the group may support customer due diligence, risk assessment and other AML/CFT decisions, but each obliged entity would remain responsible for complying with its own due diligence requirements and taking its own risk-based decisions.

Preferred option This analysis recognises that both options might entail financial and administrative costs for groups of obliged entities to ensure compliance with the new provisions of the draft RTS. In both cases, groups of obliged entities would need to set up policies and procedures for information sharing within the group and the structure, build appropriate safeguards, possibly modify their information-sharing infrastructure, and potentially adapt their compliance and governance functions to the new provisions. The exact costs would depend on the actual size and organisational structure of each obliged entity. Considering the costs and benefits described above, policy Option B was selected as the preferred option. The revisions introduced following the public consultation further strengthened this approach by linking the information-sharing framework more closely to the Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, simplifying the drafting by moving the list of information to Annex I, clarifying further the minimum operational standards for information sharing, keeping the accountability of individual obliged entities and improving operational feasibility. Overall, this approach better aligns with the objectives of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 by balancing effectiveness, proportionality, and legal certainty. Policy issue 3: degree of prescriptiveness of additional measures and supervisory actions In line with the mandate under Article 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, the draft RTS should define a Union-level response to legal impediments in third countries, including the definition of minimum actions and additional measures to be applied by the parent undertakings or obliged entities, as well as the additional supervisory actions to be applied by the supervisors of the home Member State where those additional measures prove insufficient to effectively manage ML/TF risks of subsidiaries and branches in third countries.

Under both policy options, the minimum actions are considered to provide a common baseline response to legal impediments. The policy choice therefore concerns the degree of prescriptiveness of the additional measures to be applied where those minimum actions are insufficient, and of the supervisory actions to be applied where the additional measures prove insufficient. Against this background, two policy options are considered.
A. Defining a prescriptive set of additional measures and supervisory actions.
B. Defining a set of additional measures and supervisory actions to be applied proportionately and on a risk-based basis.

Option A Under Option A, the draft RTS would define a prescriptive set of additional measures to be implemented by parent undertakings or obliged entities in the presence of legal impediments in third countries that could not be addressed by the minimum actions, accompanied by a prescriptive list of supervisory actions to be applied by supervisors once the additional measures are determined to be insufficient. The main benefit of this approach would be stronger harmonisation and enhanced supervisory convergence. A prescriptive set of additional measures would ensure harmonisation of regulatory expectations across Member States and reduce the risk of regulatory arbitrage, by ensuring that obliged entities facing similar legal impediments apply the same mitigating measures. Similarly, prescriptive supervisory actions would promote consistency in supervisory escalation and create a predictable supervisory response across the Union.

This approach would also reduce interpretative uncertainty for obliged entities at the implementation stage and facilitate compliance planning and internal governance decisions when operating in third countries where legal impediments affect the implementation of group-wide AML/CFT policies. However, these benefits would come with notable costs. First, legal impediments vary significantly across third countries. Restrictions may concern sharing and processing of customer data within the group, suspicious transaction reporting information, or supervisory access to data. Because these impediments differ in scope and severity, applying the same prescribed set of additional measures across all situations would not always be justified or proportionate.
